utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. As usual, I put the same question. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Nicholas Koumjian with Ann Sutherland and Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, along with Milka Maglov, co-counsel, and Tania Radosavljevic, legal assistant

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. And appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic. And I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you. What happened to Maitre de Roux?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maitre de Roux will join us this Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with the situation, General Talic? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I think that my counsel could be present more often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I think you have heard what General Talic said. Pass on the message to Maitre de Roux. We can't carry on like this. There's going to come a point in time when I will take further steps. Thank you, General Talic. You may sit down. I have heard that there is a slight -- not exactly problem. A small hitch with regard to one of the next -- one of the future witnesses. I think the one after this one. So I think it best to go into private session for a while. We'll discuss that particular request made by that witness before we proceed with the testimony of the current witness. Do you agree, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. I just had a couple other very small housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's start with those, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner asked me to make sure that all parties had received our list of the witnesses that we were asking 92 bis on for the Sanski Most municipality. I've confirmed with Defence counsel that they've received it. And I imagine -- I guess the Chamber has also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have at least. I suppose you have as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm now wondering if there is some recent list within the last few day that is replaced one that we got weeks ago or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. This is not weeks ago. This is last Friday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think actually we didn't file a formal notification, but we notified everyone. We just wanted to make sure that it was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All I can do is assume that I have it. I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The actual statements were handed over last week to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll check better, Mr. Koumjian, to be precise. And I suppose the Defence will do the same. Madam Fauveau, I suppose you will check too?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember, the Prosecutor gave us a list on 25th of February, containing the witness list of Sanski Most witnesses. And on that list was indicated for which witnesses they will ask the admission of statements in application of 92 bis. And if I remember well, the Defence of General Talic opposed this in a motion on the 4th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Again, could you please liaise, Mr. Koumjian, with the Defence to make sure that we are talking of the same documents. Because I'm not quite sure that we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can I just make sure by stating the witness numbers that we're requesting right now in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And these are 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Those are our applications for 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours are aware that there is pending a motion regarding 92 bis, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The guidelines --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would affect how one might deal with those. And I'm not pushing the Chamber in any way to decide it. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're not exactly very keen on -- anyway, we'll talk about it at some future point in time. But the idea of providing further guidelines is not exactly very appealing at the present moment to the Trial Chamber. But we are prepared to meet you halfway at some point in time, and we'll discuss it later on in the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The other brief matter is that Ms. Korner asked me to bring up is, last Friday we addressed the issue of the journalist and the challenge to the summons. Ms. Korner has been in contact with the counsel for the journalist. And on behalf of that counsel, she would make a -- or we are making an oral request for the transcripts. They've requested it. Rather than making them file a formal motion, Your Honour mentioned last time that either they could file a motion or we could on their behalf. I'm requesting the transcript. I think the other -- although it was in closed session, it was for the protection of the witness that the counsel is representing. So I don't see a reason that he shouldn't get the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the -- shall I consider it a request from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay so your request is being granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to identify the transcripts, as such. I suppose that you will liaise with the Registry, identify them, and those will be the transcripts that you are authorised to make available to counsel, Mr. Robinson, if I remember well, even if it is a closed session. But if it is a closed session, only in as far as it relates to Mr. Robinson's witness -- or client or clients. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just to point out, Your Honour that, the transcript indicates that Ms. Fauveau made an objection. And I know she said "no objection."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard her say "no objection." That's correct, Madam Fauveau. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Mr. President. There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. It's -- you know, sometimes it happens, when -- the moment you rose to complain about the interpretation last week. It has been happening, and happening, and happening again. Anyway, any further preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to inform the Court that we will inform counsel for the witness to be here on May the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we agreed. Making an allowance just in case we cannot meet that appointment. I think I did mention last Friday that the previous two hearings -- sittings are earmarked for the witnesses coming from particular humanitarian organisation, if I remember well. So it's a question of organising ourselves in a way such as not to get Mr. Robinson here on a Friday for nothing. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I should advise you, Your Honour, that I am today filing a motion to delay the testimony of the witnesses from the humanitarian organisation. It's prepared. It will be filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give it all due consideration, Mr. Ackerman. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland will deal with the matter regarding the witness that's come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we go into private session, please, Madam Registrar, for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Remind me. The witness we had last Friday -- the current witness is -- in public session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll go into public session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think the usher can proceed in bringing in the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Fazlagic. And welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back to this Tribunal. You are going to be handed the same document that you saw last time, and you are kindly asked to make -- to repeat your solemn declaration to tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now Ms. Sutherland from the Prosecution -- you may sit down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, for the Prosecution will continue and hopefully conclude today her examination-in-chief. And then after that, you will be cross-examined by the Defence teams. Ms. Sutherland, please. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Sutherland: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, last Friday you briefly discussed your position as director of Atlas Prima Tours. And you marked on a map Prosecution Exhibit P534A where the offices were located?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone -- yes, it is on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also drew a diagram of the area where the office is located, which is Prosecution Exhibit P535?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I inadvertently asked for this Exhibit to be marked P535, when in fact I wanted it to be marked P534B. Given that the Prosecution hasn't tendered any other exhibits since that exhibit, can the exhibit be remarked as Prosecution Exhibit P534B?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any objection on the part of the Defence? It is so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be very confusing to some lawyer trying to work on the appeal of this case to be searching around for 535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There will be a 535.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it won't be the one the transcript is referring to. It will be some other exhibit. I think it must remain 535 at this point since that's the way it's identified over and over in the transcript. One must think of a future appellant lawyer who has no idea what we are doing here other than what he can see in the transcript and so I think it has to be that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would tend to agree with Mr. Ackerman, actually, because the transcript of last Friday's sitting is not going to be changed in any case. So anyone referring to that transcript later on is going to find a reference to Exhibit 535 being. In reality, if that person looks for 535, if your request is granted, he or she will find another document. So I -- if it's no major tragedy for the Prosecution, let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then when you come to -- did you have in mind any other document already which you have marked 535 in your records?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. So that's not a major problem, I think. And we can live with 535 as it is. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified on Friday that your office was right at the very corner of the floor with a small protruding balcony. And you marked that balcony on Prosecution Exhibit 535. Which floor of the building was your office located?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first floor. On the ground floor were the counters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified on Friday that the Dubrovnik-based tourist agency Atlas had 11 employees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified that the company was disbanded and Atlas Prima Tours was set up.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of October, 1991 the firm was registered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Atlas Prima Tours commenced business, how many persons worked for the new company?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me the ethnicities of these six people, please?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I don't know how often I have to again mention ethnicities: Two Serbs, two Bosniaks, and two Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And upon the creation of the new business, why were there less people employed than in the other business? Can you explain to the Court why this was the case.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number of six people were not really fully employed because the scope of activity was significantly reduced. We just were hoping that in the immediate future things would improve, but we really didn't even need that many employees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which particular parts of the business had fallen off?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sale of railway tickets had fallen off entirely. Then also the sale of bus tickets was reduced by about 90 per cent. Programmes of travel and holidays and weekend excursions had almost completely died out, so that we were just meting out an existence. Only barely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people that worked on the rail counter?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of the persons working at the rail counter were Serbs by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they given full-time employment when the new company was commenced?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that counter in the new company wasn't operating at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other people that weren't given full-time employment, why did they -- was there any reason why they left the company?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plane ticket counter's business was halved, so that only one person was kept to man that counter, and assistance at the airplane counter later when the sale of plane tickets increased was provided by employees from the commercial department. They passed the test to be able to work at that counter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone retire?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A lady who also used to work at the rail ticket counter, Mrs. Nada Ojdenic, left. And when a list was made by those who were making lists, was marked as being Serbian, but she was in fact Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people that weren't given full-time employment, were they still kept on by the company in some shape or form?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the employees who was considered to be redundant and declared as such, I think immediately took a bonus consisting of 24 monthly salaries. And another colleague got a job in the Territorial Defence staff. And the two others, that is, Mrs. Nada Crljenica, and Mrs. Stanka Vukomanovic, were both taken over by us as laid off workers. But they enjoyed all entitlements as if they were employed in Atlas Prima Tours. And then Mrs. Nada Crljenica was fully employed again soon after that, and she in fact became the manager of the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person who got the job at the National Defence Secretariat, what was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragoljub Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the laid-off workers enjoyed all the entitlements. Does this mean that their health cover was covered by the agency?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you encounter any problems later on because you made these staff redundant?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any correspondence from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you receive a letter from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First the media launched a campaign against me. And in several installments, journalist Ratko Maric and Mrs. Bozic, I think her name was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. If you could just pause there. Did you receive a letter in December 1991 from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received a letter in which I'm accused of having fired workers, all of whom were of Serb ethnicity, which was not true, and that I should adjust that decision, that I should behave in accordance with a certain ratio, which I didn't fully comprehend in fact. I reacted to this in conversations with certain people in the municipality. I wanted them to show me and prove to me what they meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you receive this letter from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the letter from Mr. Rajko Kasagic, the president of the Executive Council of Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier about the media.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an article written in the Glas newspaper about this matter?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was precisely in Glas that in several copies, they -- several issues, they wrote about me, carrying certain data of their own. And on a number of occasions, I tried to disprove that. In fact, all the employed in the new company, Atlas Prima Tours -- and I repeat again, all the employed, which means both Serbs, Croats, and a Bosniak, apart from myself, because I was not a signatory of that letter. They absolutely rejected the allegations that had been made prior to that in the Glas newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall who was making the initial accusations in the paper?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first were launched by these two reporters. And then eventually at the end of those accusations and these reports in the media, sometime in April, I read a surprising article, a report on the -- a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Province of Krajina, intimating who would be among the next to be persecuted and fired. And among these, my name was referred to as being a drastic case, saying that this could not go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before we move on to that, did you speak to anyone in authority regarding the situation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of my -- one of the people closest to me at the time in the municipality was Mr. Branko Cvijic, who was secretary of the Municipal Assembly. And I tried to talk to him in the context of our previous relationship. I asked him to clarify things for me. However, I did not get much encouragement from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the time period this was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must have been around -- actually, after those news reports, so around the end of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you say to Mr. Cvijic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to provide documents in support of what I was saying, that the things that I was being criticised for did not apply. Branko Cvijic knew very well who I was, what my ideological positions were, who I was and what I represented in that town. I tried to make it clear to him that that could not be said of me, that my positions were not such. However, it was logical to me that I could not expect from him an answer that would support me, so that I simply tried to ease and air my feelings, hoping I would feel better afterwards. But I knew that there was really nothing I could do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Cvijic recommend to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He recommended at the end of this conversation -- and at that point in time, I thought also that that was the only solution -- that I should -- that the situation would calm down, at least to some extent with respect to me, of course, if among the employees of Serb ethnicity I were to appoint a person as manager and that I should withdraw from that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do as Mr. Cvijic recommended?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, immediately. That same day, I called up Mrs. Nada Crljenica. I invited her to a talk with me. We discussed matters for about one hour. I explained to her the situation, that I must say I myself found myself in. And I said, "Madam Nada, you probably are aware of the times we are living in, so I ask you to take over my position, and we'll see what will be with me." And then I was appointed advisor to the company, and Mrs. Nada took over as manager, so that this proposal of Mr. Branko Cvijic was immediately implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the first time in that situation -- and I also hope the last time. Shall I tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day I was called up by an employee in the crime department of SUP. I immediately got into the car and went there. When I reached the office I was told to go to, I saw a former student of mine. Because by occupation, I'm a teacher, so that I had a number of former students in these various services. And the conversation centred around something that allegedly we were selling tickets for international bus transport and for foreign currency, which we were not allowed to do I said, "That's the first time I hear of it. We have all the necessary licences to be able to do that, a licence, as it appeared in the Official Gazette, which said we could do it with the appropriate contracts." And he asked me to provide the relevant documents. My employees immediately brought the necessary document, but he wanted a recent document. And then by telex, I quickly received from Livno the latest document which I provided. But in the meantime, I was left in the room several times alone, because this employee said he went to fetch something. And this would take two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that it looked to me as if ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As if something like brainwashing. I was there all day. In the end, they couldn't find anything that I could be reproached for. And I was told everything was okay. But nevertheless, his parting words were "take care." After saying that, I asked, "What should I take care about?" And that is how we parted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was happening just around the month of April, the month that proved to be crucial for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your testimony that you read a surprising report. And you started to tell us what that report was about. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When my name was mentioned? Is that what you're referring to? Oh, yes. Yes. Glas would regularly publish the main conclusions from meetings of the Crisis Staff and also the decisions taken by the Crisis Staff. But most of those reports consisting of naming certain people, certain employees, certain companies -- of course mostly of non-Serb ethnicity -- according to which, as we saw it, these intimated steps that would be taken against those people in the future. And on that day, two or three names were mentioned, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what was said in the article about yourself and who said it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I remember perfectly. In block letters, highlighted, my name was highlighted, and Mr. Brdjanin was quoted as saying that a special case was the director of Atlas, Ibrahim Fazlagic, who had fired six workers, all of them being of Serb ethnicity. And then something that discouraged me most -- not discouraged, because I was -- knew what the truth was. He went on to say that this could not be tolerated, which meant that I had already been condemned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 165 [Realtime transcript read in error "615"]. The transcript reads Prosecution Exhibit 615. It should be 165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct, Ms. Sutherland. If we can have that corrected straight away, it will be much better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, is this the article that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the English translation would be placed on the ELMO machine.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the article, with a very clear title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. On my monitor, I'm seeing the English translation of the article carried in Glas. I suppose -- yes. But I suppose since we also have a copy of Glas, what the witness should be shown and what should appear on the ELMO is the photocopy of the article from Glas, not the English translation, even though he speaks English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has the Glas article in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. But perhaps he could -- we could put it on the ELMO, and he can show us on the ELMO which is the article. Because here I see a lot of articles. I don't understand the language. It's in Cyrillic script. And perhaps he can point it out to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you just tell the Court the date of this newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the date on the top left-hand corner of the page?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the 28th of April, or is it the 30th of April and the 1st and 2nd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th; of the article itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this news was published.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is the article -- yes, yes. Which is the article that's referring -- that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Only personnel loyal to the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you see this article for the first time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your reaction to it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My private reaction was that was the end of the story, that I hadn't -- no place -- that there was no place for me. Though even then I couldn't believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Atlas Prima Tours sell airline tickets to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when -- do you recall when JAT, the Yugoslav airline organised airline flights from Banja Luka to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not the exact date. But this was particularly pronounced in the months of April and May. Even, I think, at the end of March. But in April, up to the 18th of May, when the last plane left for Belgrade, there was a great deal of interest. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many flights a day were there from Banja Luka to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On an average, there were two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were buying these tickets?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and as I saw it, tickets were being bought mainly -- or one might say 100 per cent, by non-Serbs. And of course, they were one-way tickets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were non-Serbs buying tickets to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, it was the only way to get out of Banja Luka, because virtually all other means of transportation for other countries could not be used. Trains had stopped a long time ago, and the last bus to leave Banja Luka for Croatia was at the beginning of April, and it didn't go from Banja Luka but from Prijedor. So some passengers managed to get as far as a crossroads the near Banja Luka where they got onto that bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last train from Banja Luka to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last train for Croatia, I think, was at the end of 1991. At the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was the last train from Banja Luka to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I took that train. It was one of the last to leave -- at the beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were non-Serbs wanting to leave Banja Luka in March, April, May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an awful lot of pressure applied. First, more or less they all remained without their jobs. Then there was intimidation that went on, constant pressure, applied in different ways: On the phone, in personal contacts. Simply this atmosphere, as far as the non-Serb population was concerned, it was unbearable, and in that period, the only way to save oneself, and one's family was to leave the town. And naturally, when politicians named people, that -- saying that there was no -- there was no place for us in that town, when they stated that, it was a sign that we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the tickets were only issued one way. What was the price of a one-way ticket?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it wasn't more than 100 Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of tickets being sold for a higher price?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not, but certainly there was a reselling of ticket, I presume. At the airport, as -- while I was still going there, nobody was asking about the name. It was important to show a ticket at the check-in and then go through the military and the police check, and then one would be lucky enough to get onto the plane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did JAT, the Yugoslav airline, ever -- did any staff ever work out of your office?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two employees whom I knew very well. I don't know their names, because they came to see me as part of a -- a business visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this time that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the same period in question, particularly in April and May. So they came to see us, to -- so to speak the check the sale. And then for a while, in Hotel Bosna, they took a room. And from there, they started selling tickets individually from that room for that flight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... selling tickets from your offices?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that room, they came to me without asking any questions, without any consultations, whether they can do it or not. They took over a counter, and they were selling tickets. I understand why they did it; so that the money -- because the money -- the tickets were bought for foreign currency, so that the money would then be wired to Belgrade -- or rather, not wired. But in fact, the daily profit -- the daily turnover, they would take money by car so that another JAT representative would be waiting and the money would be going directly through to Belgrade. So this was no longer going through the public auditing service as we had done it until then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... during the end of April and the 18th of May when you said that the last flight to Belgrade occurred, in your estimation, how many tickets per day was your company selling?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that was the high season. And in our branch office, in a rough estimate, I think that on a daily basis up to 300 tickets were sold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time you went to the airport?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was normal that occasionally -- not always -- but it was normal that I should go every two or three days. I would escort groups because about three buses would leave the branch. And so then I would go, as some kind of a guide. I would take them to the airport, as head of the convoy. But on one day -- I believe that it was the beginning of May -- I was stopped by the police on the entrance to the airport, and they said that I was no longer allowed to get in and told me to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 179, which is the ARK Crisis Staff conclusion of the 8th of May, 1992. P179 is also part of Exhibit 227 which is the entire Official Gazette, number 2, of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher, if the English translation could be put on the ELMO, showing paragraph number 7 of the document. And also the next page -- the top of the next page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever receive a copy of this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever told by the authorities that you couldn't sell tickets?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness now be shown Prosecution Exhibit 181, which is a Glas article dated the 9th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3, there is a report from the session of the Autonomous Region Krajina War Staff dated the 8th of May. If I can take you to the second paragraph. "The possibility of abuse was also considered --" I'm sorry. Earlier, "Atlas and Putnik enterprises who sell tickets as they wish, without taking into account the seriousness of the present situation at all. The possibility of abuse was also considered, so an order was issued that in future tickets for flights to Belgrade cannot be sold without the approval of the National Defence Council or the war staffs. In case of non-compliance, all those responsible in Atlas and Putnik will suffer very severe penalties, said Radoslav Brdjanin, president of the Bosnian Krajina War Staff in today's meeting with journalists." Did you ever see this article?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told this Chamber a moment ago that you were never told by the authorities that you couldn't sell tickets. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Officially, I was never told.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown Prosecution Exhibit 183, which is an ARK Crisis Staff conclusion of the 9th of May. Paragraph 6, in particular.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Due to its abuses in its work, the Atlas travel agency is prohibited from further work." And then it continues. Did you ever receive a copy of this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Glas article that you saw a moment ago, it talked about abuses, allegations of selling airline tickets to military-age persons or for too much money. Did your agency ever sell tickets for more than 100 Deutschmarks, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one of my employees ever did such a thing. This can be checked with the current employees. I believe they're now called Krajina Turist. They used to work for me. And they can be asked to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Rajko Kasagic ever ask you for airline tickets?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what time period this was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same period of time. At the end of April, perhaps first days of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He called me on the phone to go and see him. I did not know what it was about, because I know Mr. Kasagic well and he knows me. And I went to see him to the executive board. I went into his office straight away. We had a coffee. And he then told me that he needed, I think -- I can't promise you that I'm telling the truth -- but perhaps five tickets for his own needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say why? Why he wanted the five tickets?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me. But I'm not sure whether that was that. But he said that it was either his brother that -- he was married to a Bosniak woman, and that he wanted to send them away to a safe place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you provide them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally I -- of course I would do that, because I know -- I knew Mr. Kasagic. I went back to the branch and I asked -- I think this was Mrs. Crljenica or perhaps Rada. But I asked them if they could get these five tickets. And Mr. Kasagic also gave me the names and that they would take it -- take them to him. And that's what they did -- to Mr. Kasagic, to Mr. Kasagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, did you ever receive a decision to cease the work of the travel agency?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of the decision?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you receive this letter?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received it by mail. I think it was some kind of internal mail. I know that one of my employees brought it to me from the counter. He brought it to my office upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 532, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I should make a small correction. This was beginning of June, beginning of June. I said beginning of May. It's a slip of the tongue. Actually, it should be beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, who is the signature block on that decision?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the signature of the president, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court who issued the decision and what the decision says.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was issued by the Crisis Staff of the ARK, and it says that the Atlas agency, Prima Tours, ceases with its activities and that the business premises will be taken over by the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, which has absolutely no legal grounds. There's no legal basis for it. What I found incredible, although I'm not a lawyer but I do I understand some things -- there wasn't one single sentence of giving any reasons for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any explanation as to why it had been sent?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or anyone ever discuss this decision with anyone from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There was some kind of mini delegation on the very same day when we got this decision. They went to look for Mr. Brdjanin. They waited for him for a long time in the corridor. I know where that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Who were the people that went to speak to the authorities?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can remember it well, it was Nada -- Rada Dobra. There was Tijana Crnic, and I think Mirsada Gradanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rada Dobra, is she of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Tijana Crnic, is she also of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mirsada Gradanin?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did they speak to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted to speak to Mr. Brdjanin personally. And according to what they told me, after an hour Mr. Brdjanin, either upon coming into the premises or leaving them, he simply told the that he cannot discuss anything on this subject any more. And so they came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basically he said the decision was final.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that was not the witness's testimony. That was the Prosecutor's statement. The witness did not say that he said the decision was final. The witness said he said he couldn't discuss anything further. And I object to the Prosecutor putting words in the witness's mouth in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After receiving this decision, were you stopped from going to work?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. And for a while, we continued to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point, were you stopped from going to work?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how you were stopped by force?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came one morning at 7.00 a.m. And in front of the door with -- the office with the counters. And for a while already there were reserve policemen placed in front of the counters. So one policeman whom I knew -- his name was Zoran -- he told me that I could no longer get inside. That was a shock for me. My employees from behind the counter looked at me, and I -- I looked down, and I went back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else stopped from entering -- from working on that day?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your employment officially terminated?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, no, not yet, until I received from my colleague, whom I appointed as director -- as manager, until I received the decision on the cessation of employment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what date you received this document, the date of the decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, you can show him the documents straight away and proceed with asking him whether he confirms that that is the document that officially terminated his employment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 533.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, who has signed that document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mrs. Nada Crljenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please read the decision to the Court.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Decision on the termination of employment. The employment of Ibrahim Fazlagic, advisor --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you can please pause there. Can you please start from the top of the document and read the text --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, okay. [Interpretation] "Based on a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Banja Luka, decision number 03-531/92 of 22 June 1992, I hereby issue a decision on the termination of employment. The employment of Ibrahim Fazlagic, advisor at the Atlas Prima Tours travel agency, Banja Luka, is terminated as of 30 June 1992. Statement of reasons: Since Ibrahim Fazlagic is carrying out the duties and assignments of advisor at the Atlas Prima Tours travel agency, Banja Luka, in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina, Banja Luka, number 03-531/92, it was decided as in the disposition of the decision."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 26th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, the ARK Crisis Staff decision number 03-531/92 is also Prosecution Exhibit 254 and 255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed to something different -- I mean, I'm not stopping you now. But just before you proceed to the next series of questions, just let me know, because I would like to have something clarified with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, was the position of director of a travel agency seen as being a highly sensitive government position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were no elements whatsoever that this should be considered as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you appeal this decision?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was more a question of formality, because I deeply believed that it was so, just a formality, which would not give any results. I spoke to Mrs. Nada Crljenica at the branch office. I asked her, "What does that mean in the statement of reasons?" And she said that this was because I was working on the work which is to do with sending and receiving information. Naturally, ironically, I asked, "Is a kind of information when the train is leaving or plane leaving? Are there any excursions to Dubrovnik? Is this -- is this the kind of information that is so important that on their basis, I am being dismissed from my job?"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland -- And Witness, please follow what I am going to tell Ms. Sutherland, because you will be asked to clarify later on. Looking at Exhibit P181, there is in the second paragraph a reference to two enterprises. One is Atlas, the other one is Putnik. Now, in the original Glas report, actually you will find the words "Atlasa" and "Putnika," then in the Exhibit number P183, at the bottom of the page, you have the decision of the War Staff, decision number 6, to which reference was made earlier, deciding that Atlas travel agency is prohibited from further work, followed immediately by another decision, in the same context, that the Putnik travel agency shall be allowed to sell tickets for flights to Belgrade. Now, I know that there might -- there probably is a very simple explanation to what I'm going to say, namely that probably Putnika is a B/C/S word for "travel." But I see on the face of the B/C/S Exhibit P533, just beneath the signature -- the name and signature of Nada Crljenica, the words "Putnika Agencija." And in the logo, at the top of the page, also there is "Putnika Agencija." I would like you to direct a question to the witness to make sure that this Putnika Agencija in this document must not and is not to be confused with the Putnika enterprise that was allowed to continue trading tickets to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, did you hear what His Honour just said? Did you understand?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This stamp that appears on the bottom of Prosecution Exhibit 533, the decision by Nada Crljenica to dismiss you from employment, are you familiar with that stamp that's on the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he ought to be shown the document again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought he had it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You should, can he be shown Exhibit 533.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that stamp at the bottom of the document, where it says --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I worked on it. In fact, I had it done. I had the stamp made when we founded the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your company is called Atlas Prima Tours. Why is the word "Putnika" agency also on the stamp?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Atlas Prima Tours could be a commercial establishment. It could be a factory. It could be anything. But Atlas Prima Tours is a travel agency, which in B/C/S is "Putnika Agencija".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was another company by the name of Putnika which was in competition with you, with your company, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Putnik is a separate company, with headquarters in Belgrade. This was a branch office. Again of another travel agency called Putnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That clarifies everything for me. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I have been misinformed. I was -- I understood on Friday that we were going back to the old break system and that we would be breaking now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not really. Not today. We are stopping for about five minutes to give time to the technicians to change the tapes and then we continue as before, at least for today. And then I'm going to discuss it further tomorrow, because there is a technical hitch that the tapes only last for one hour and 40 minutes, and they have to be changed. And therefore, time is required for that. So in actual fact, we will be stopping in -- Madam Registrar, in a couple of minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Seven minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In seven minutes, yes. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I had also understood -- and maybe I was -- misheard -- that part of the problems we've been having with translation is that the translators have been getting too tired during these long sessions and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We can -- I have no problems at all in reverting to the old regime, the previous regime, finishing at 7.00, instead of 6.30. I frankly don't know how much difference half an hour makes, but I'm prepared to accommodate everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I love leaving at 6.30, Your Honour. I was thinking a couple of 15-minute breaks would make more sense and we could still leave at 6.30. I don't know whether that works or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I said I would be discussing it again tomorrow, because I haven't had a chance to discuss it with my colleagues to start with. Today we agreed with Madam Registrar, who came to see me three minutes before I was proceeding to come up here to tell me about the problem. And I said -- actually, she offered to leave everything as it was today and then we will discuss further tomorrow and make any adjustments that may become necessary. So Ms. Sutherland, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering whether I can get through the next topic in what's now probably four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can stop here for the agreed five minutes so that the technicians change the tapes and continue soon after and then we will have the break. Unless you prefer to have a break straight away now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think that's probably the most sensible course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break now. I think that's more sensible. We'll have a break now for 25 -- for 30 minutes. And then we'll take it up from there. Thank you. Yes. The witness can be escorted out of the courtroom, please. So we'll break for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness, please. Why is it taking so long? Mr. Ackerman, I'm more or less basing on what you've heard so far. How long do you anticipate your cross-examination will last -- or will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm guessing probably not more than two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think less than an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And -- okay. Thank you. And how long do you think you need the witness on examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Probably another half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. So you can plan with starting with the next witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if you will be examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, before the break, you said that Atlas Prima Tours turned into Krajina Turist. Do you recall when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That occurred towards the end of June. I don't know the exact date, because I no longer went to work in the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who worked in Krajina Turist, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Nada Crljenica stayed on, and Mrs. Rada Dobra. I'm not sure about Mrs. Stanka Vukomanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, what ethnicity are these people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you about other travel agencies in Banja Luka. You mentioned earlier the Putnik agency. Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the ground floor, close to the lobby of the Bosna Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just one more question on Krajina Turist. Do you recall who set that -- that agency up?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'm not mistaken, I think it was formed by the executive council. I saw in Glas a small framed report in which the board of management of Krajina Turist -- two people were appointed to that board. I remember the name of only one, Mr. Dusko Lasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to Putnik, what was their main business in 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly selling air tickets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anyone who worked there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. One of my staff members switched to Putnik, Mr. Hamdija Trnovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his position at Putnik? A. He was also in charge of the Putnik branch office, the travel agency Putnik of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did he work at Putnik, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, for about three years. Three, four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other -- any other travel agencies operating during this time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, yes. But many, because there was no business, simply died out. For instance, Unis, Inex; I remember those two. Simply because of the situation they found themselves in, they closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you some questions about life in Banja Luka. Can you describe to the Court the atmosphere in Banja Luka in 1992, up until the time that you left.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us -- and I have to say for a part of the Serbs too, the atmosphere was very difficult because there was already shortages of electricity in the first place. A large number of people would spend the day in front of their apartment buildings where they improvised cooking stoves, and they cooked outside and spent their time outside. And for us, this was a period of uncertainty, of constant fear of what tomorrow would bring. But nevertheless, we never believed that anything drastic could happen, and that applies to me too and many of my friends. We thought that this was just a storm that would pass quickly. Unfortunately, we were naive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if any, restrictions were in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean power cuts, yes, there were power shortages and cuts, and that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed. Around the beginning of April one morning -- actually, this is linked to the appearance of SOS -- checkpoints were erected at the entrance to the town. Before that, several buildings were placed under control. For instance, the Banja Luka radio station, the municipal assembly building, and some other facilities. My wife one morning on her way to work by car was stopped at a bridge near the student's hostel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already testified in relation to your wife being stopped by the SOS.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the mosques in Banja Luka damaged in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was an explosion at the Ferhadija Mosque. And as a citizen, I was interested to see what had happened in the morning, so I went there and I saw it. But obviously this was just the beginning, because there were no significant damage. No significant damage had been done at that time. But there were other activities, especially regarding private businesses, coffee-shops, and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just describe for the Court what happened to these private businesses and coffee-shops.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close to where my agency was, there was like a crafts centre with a large number of small businesses, services, ranging from coffee bars, shoe repairs, photographers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who owned these businesses?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All ethnicities were represented. But explosives were thrown only at businesses owned by non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was this occurring?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time, almost every evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you listened to the radio. Did the music stay the same throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a drastic change in programming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you notice this change?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime simultaneously with these blockades, if I can call them that, or when these businesses were placed under control that was when the music programme of Radio Banja Luka was completely changed. I think for a time, the editor of the music programme was also the director. I'm not quite sure. His name is Mr. Kenjalovic. I heard this from others that he was explicitly ordered, and I think personally, by Mr. Vukic. When one morning he went to Radio Banja Luka, he said that no music can be aired except the music that suited them. And indeed, in the morning, we listened to that music and no other, that day and the days that followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of music was this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, please don't misunderstand me. I find it very difficult to say this, because I used to listen to that music before too, music of all peoples but I must say in this case, it was Serbian music.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, a moment ago you mentioned that Hamdija Trnovac who worked at the Putnik agency worked there for approximately three to four years. Do you recall when he left the agency, what month, and year?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left roughly at the same time as I did, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he left?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply one morning he arrived and found the premises locked and from them, a lot of equipment had been taken out. And as he personally told me, he simply saw that he could no longer work there. He picked up his things, his personal affairs, and went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he receive any official notification as to why he couldn't enter the premises?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. He didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, when did you leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, 1992, in a very strange way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to leaving Banja Luka, did you see the mayor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recount for the Court the conversation that you had with the mayor of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt a very strong need, even desire, to meet with three people from my Banja Luka whom I knew very well and with whom I had cooperated. That is archbishop Jefrem, the town mayor Radic, and somebody we had a lot of respect for until then at least, as an intellectual, Mr. Gugo Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me the conversation you had with Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With both Radic and Jefrem and Lazarevic, I discussed the same subject. I simply wished to express my reaction, my position, and my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. question as to why. So I roughly said the following: "Even on my death bed I will not understand why I left my town to which I had dedicated 40 years of my life, much more than many others, than even those who are sitting here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Radic's response, if any?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I knew Mr. Radic very well -- I'd known him for a long time, for I too had been involved in football for many years. I was on the board of the Borac Football Club, and Mr. Radic was a junior who played in Borac. We all called him Prede. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this he has touched upon already, and if I remember well he even said that they were very happy when he was appointed mayor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may direct the witness to something else, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you can just tell the Court what, if anything, Mr. Radic said to you in relation to the conversation you had with him just prior to leaving Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, he was probably embarrassed, in view of the fact that we had lived through some fine times together, that we had spent together in our city. And I say "our city," on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... having been asked twice to say what did Mr. Radic say to you. Again he's going off on their times together and that sort of thing. Could he be instructed to simply answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm going to interrupt you, because you interrupted the witness, who was, according to me, just about to start answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You may be right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, if you look at his statement, the written statement, that I am sure you have, he started off by saying that Mr. Radic had -- was looking down. And here he is saying "at that point in time, he was probably embarrassed, in view of the fact --" he was just about to start answering the question. So please. My apologies. Start -- answer the question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was a very simple one. Ms. Sutherland wanted to know what Mr. Radic said to you in relation to the conversation you had with him just prior -- just before you had to leave, or you to decided leave Banja Luka. I mean, more or less we want the gist, the substance of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] I was just about to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radic, with his head bowed, tried to explain to me that I should have understanding for the current situation that this would pass, and that I should be aware that this would not last, that that was how things were now and that I should reconcile myself to that current situation. Something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say that you would eventually get over it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in so many words, but rather that this was a time that we would put behind us very soon. But obviously he was mistaken in his estimate. Maybe that was indeed what he thought and what he hoped for but obviously other options got the upper hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago that you left Banja Luka in a strange way. Can you very briefly describe for the Court how you left Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not obtain permission to leave the city. And due to various circumstances, one day I met a neighbour of mine who -- and unfortunately I have to say this, he was of Serb ethnicity, but he was a good acquaintance of mine. And he was in such a position as to be able to make it possible for me to get on a military convoy which was heading for Belgrade. This was a time when through the corridor via Brcko and Bijeljina -- and I have to say this, at least on the basis of the information I had, a non-Serb could not pass alive. And I fulfilled just one condition that this gentleman set and that was to get a doctor's referral for treatment in Belgrade. This was not a problem for me because I was on very good terms with virtually all Banja Luka's doctors. So I got that referral note. And so in agreement with him, I arrived in front of the barracks and he asked me when I get to that place that I pretend not to know him. And of course I agreed to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you went to Belgrade, and from there you went to a third country; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I managed along the journey to make a deviation towards Novi Sad, and spending the night in Novi Sad. After that I headed for Hungary, and via Hungary I got to Virovitica, because you couldn't pass through Croatia. There was fierce fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you managed to reunite with your family in a third country.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were in Banja Luka, or at any time, did you own a weapon?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could just wait there for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Now, sir, the Prosecution has finished with its set of questions. It's now the turn of the first team -- the first Defence team; that's the Defence team for accused Radoslav Brdjanin. And you are going to be cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, twice today I have forgotten to pass these. And I apologise. It's the List of Documents that I'm going to use on cross. There are only two documents, and you've seen both of them and you're familiar with both of them. And I think -- I'm not sure, but I think they're probably both available to you. And I'm sorry about forgetting to hand these out earlier this morning. Those are for the Judges; that's for the Prosecutor. I don't know if I can -- I don't know if I can hear -- yes. I think it's probably on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes? You can hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
