utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to begin my examination of you by asking you about the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor. It was a statement that you gave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, are you comfortable in that position, or -- is it a position of your choice?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, no. But I don't know where else to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Isn't there space over there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This works pretty good, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Provided you are comfortable. But that way you're not exactly facing the witness. Anyway, go ahead. If you're happy, so are we.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm almost always happy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Almost always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The difficulty would be trying to move this over there. I don't think that can be done because of the wires and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, this courtroom is a little bit awkward. For example, to talk to you or to look at you or to observe you, I literally have to look to the degree of 45 degrees at least, which is no good. I mean, you're not directly in my field of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we'll just do the best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the Prosecutor on the 28th and 29th of May, 2001 to representatives of the Prosecutor's office; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have had occasion since your arrival here in The Hague to be given that statement and to have an opportunity to review it, have you not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have mentioned to us as you began your testimony here on Friday that there were some things that you discovered in going through that statement that you wanted to change. And we noted those changes. You recall doing that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since that time, have you noticed any additional changes that you would like to make to that statement before I begin to ask you questions about it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that you stand by the balance of your statements contained within that document?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other thing I want to ask you about is the testimony that you gave here on Friday and so far today. Reflecting back on that, is there anything that you have told the Chamber on Friday or today that on reflection you believe you might have been mistaken about and would like to change?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, you -- I'm going to talk initially about your testimony from Friday. That's the first subject I want to discuss with you. I'm going to refer to page 76 and 77 of the LiveNote version of the transcript of your testimony. You were talking, you will recall, sir, about the information centre that was in the municipality building in Banja Luka. You recall talking about that. And --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- you were asked when was the first time you saw this information centre. And you said "when it was inaugurated. I wouldn't know the exact year." You gave the name of someone who was the municipal president. "It must have been somewhere in the 1970s, the end of the 1970s." And then you were asked, "Was this the only room to the information centre?" And your answer was, "No. Inside, in it, there were two or three other rooms with printers, fax machines, telex machines. And for those -- at those times it was considered to be the most modern such facility in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, are you referring to that time at the end of the 1970s when the -- there was the public celebration about it being opened?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was during -- it was during the time of that public inauguration that you had an opportunity to see all of the things that were inside that room?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that you did not have occasion to visit that room at a later occasion, that it was not a room that was open to the public.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't open to the public, but I was chef de cabinet. And with many visitors, guests, I went to see this room, to have a look at the premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So up until what year would you have had access to what was -- to see that room and see the things that were in it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until 1981?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the room contained fax machines; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fax and telex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that fax machines did not come into public use until the end of the 1980s, around 1990?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall that. But perhaps it's from those years that I remember it. But there was certainly a telex machine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask that the Prosecutor to provide you with a copy of your witness statement, because I now want to ask you some questions about it. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you want to continue in English?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I have a suspicion that you understand every question I ask you in English before you hear the translation. You speak on page 3 of the English version of your statement of a situation that had developed in the newspapers and otherwise that was distressing to you. And you indicate that sometime in April of 1992 you went to see Branko Cvijic in his office. You talked about that a little earlier today; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his recommendation to you regarding a solution regarding the problems that you were speaking to him about was that you appoint a Serb as the director of Atlas Prima Tours, which you then did; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person that was appointed as director or acting director, I believe, was this woman Nada Crljenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And between the time that you had reduced the number of employees from 11 to 6, Nada Crljenica had been not working full time at Atlas Prima Tours. She was brought back to be the acting director; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you came back -- when she came back, you were made -- you were made an advisor to the firm, were you not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who appointed you as advisor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in talking to Madam Nada -- and I believe that Madam Rada was also there. They simply asked me what I -- what position I should occupy. So we came up with this idea that I should be given this position of advisor, because I couldn't get any other specific position. I am not trained to work at the counter. I used to be a manager. And in order to help their work in advising her, in order for her to carry out her duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was your idea, then, that you become an advisor, or was it theirs?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a joint idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall who suggested it first?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, these JAT flights that were going from Banja Luka to Belgrade that you've been testifying about, those flights were organised and started operating, I believe you said in your statement, in March or April of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that it was virtually all Muslims and Croats that were booking flights and buying tickets to fly on those flights to Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that at that time, in May I believe it was or maybe even earlier, the military personnel who were not born in Bosnia-Herzegovina had been transferred back to Serbia and that many of the people who were buying tickets and flying on those flights were families of the military personnel that had been sent back to Serbia? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a very small number, because they used different flight, a different plane. It had a nickname Kikas. That was the plane and the wounded took to get to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the families of the soldiers, not the soldiers themselves; their families. Their families were flying on this -- these JAT flights from Banja Luka to Belgrade, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember them buying tickets from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Serb families buying tickets from you for their sons who were subject to conscription to get them out of the area so they wouldn't have to fight? And weren't there a number of those kinds of people flying on that flight?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that in our agency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have talked already about the company Atlas being shut down. You said on page 5 in the English version of your statement: "In my opinion, Atlas Prima Tours were shut down solely because it was associated to a Croatian company, and its company director was a Bosniak." Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the second part of that, at least, can't be true because the company director at that point was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But before that, I had been the director precisely at that critical moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other travel agency that was selling tickets to Belgrade eventually was shut down also, wasn't it? Putnik.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was not a Croatian company, was it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the director was Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a Belgrade company, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the flights to Belgrade by JAT ended, I think you say, approximately 18 May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these agencies that were selling tickets to flights to Belgrade, I take it they weren't shut down because nobody wanted to leave Banja Luka anymore. I assume people still wanted to fly to Belgrade, that there was still a demand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that most of those who wanted to leave Banja Luka as soon as possible, they had all probably gone by the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll accept that. On page 7 of your statement in the English version, you say this: "I know that Brdjanin was the main propagandist for the SDS in 1991 and 1992." That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know this? Did somebody from the SDS tell you that Brdjanin was their main propagandist?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Banja Luka, everybody knew this through different types of information that came to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about everybody. I'm talking about you. How did you know this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew through statements and stories that people told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Statements by who? Did someone tell you that Brdjanin was the main propagandist for SDS?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several people told me this, people who were close to the authorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were SDS people who would know who told you this; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they were members of the SDS, but they were also members of the Serbian people who gave us certain information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us the names of -- let's just make it two -- two people that told you that Brdjanin was the main propagandist for the SDS in 1991 and 1992, just two.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say the name of Slobodan Kustrinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. But I think also, Mr. Dusan Lajisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kustrinovic, Slobodan Kustrinovic, how would he have been in a position to know about Mr. Brdjanin? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a director of the company Cajevec, he was also close to the organs of authority. I also saw him enter the building of the municipal assembly at that time probably for some talks with other businessmen. So at that time I had a very unpleasant interview with Mr. Kustrinovic and Mr. Lajisic in front of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position would Dusan Lajisic have been in to give you this information?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also close to the authorities. He was director of the Banja Luka Brewery and he was also there. So one time after a meeting at the municipality, I met him -- I met them in front of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What brewery was he director of? Would that be the brewery that is currently in operation in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Banja Luka Brewery, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Kustrinovic is deceased?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us somebody else that you heard from that Mr. Brdjanin was the main propagandist for the SDS that is not deceased?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What proof do you have, what knowledge do you have, that Mr. Brdjanin was even a member of the SDS in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you were talking about a period of time, your statement about Mr. Brdjanin spoke of 1991 and 1992. And you say then after that, that you remember an interview that he gave in March -- perhaps March of 1992, and then you make this statement: "During this same period, I remember that Dr. Vukic forbade playing all types of music with the exception of Serb music on Radio Banja Luka," this same period being the spring -- late 1991 and early 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when was it that you became -- when was it that Dr. Vukic told the radio station to stop playing Serb music?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So non-Serb music was still being played all the way up until the beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even before that. It was rather reduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it reduced in March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that drastically, but significantly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If anyone contended that the radio station was not permitted to play Serb music in late 1991 and early 1992, they'd be incorrect, I take it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If anyone says that the radio station was not permitted to play non-Serb music in late 1991 or early 1992, that person would be incorrect; is that correct? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person would be saying the correct things, at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they weren't permitted to play non-Serb music at that point; only Serb music.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time in 1991, there was different types of music. I'm talking about the period prior to the blockade of Radio Banja Luka and just before, even before the blockade there was significantly less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I knew you were. You -- I obviously did not ask my question properly, causing you not to understand it. And I apologise. My question was this: If someone says that you're incorrect, that the playing of non-Serb music was banned from Radio Banja Luka in late 1991 and early 1992, I take it that it's your position that that person is not telling -- is wrong, is mistaken?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is that at the end of 1991 and the first days of 1992, this was not banned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And someone who says it was is not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Ackerman, you are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- you're phrasing your question in a way which either for the translators it is a little bit difficult to -- to translate or it's a little bit difficult or confusing for the witness to -- not to understand but to reply to, because the way the question is put -- I think it could be rephrased. I mean, if you ask -- let me ask the question. Let's take April 1992. If I say in April of 1992, the playing of non-Serb music on Banja Luka radio station was banned; is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I say the same thing, but only in regard to March 1992, is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But as I said, there was some -- some significant changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We're heading that way. And in February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was done by the people in the programme themselves, their own initiative. And in February, what I said was on their -- of their own will. It was within the radio station that they had done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go now to November or December 1991. What difference would you say there would be in the playing of non-Serb music between November and December 1991 and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed now. You've got your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour. I appreciate you clearing that up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on -- I want to go through some documents with you. And I think most of these have been talked about on direct examination, although I'm unsure about the exhibit numbers with regard to some of them, so I might need some help from the Prosecutor. The first document I want to talk to you about is a document that is attached to your statement as attachment number 7. Do you have the attachments to your statement there in front of you? And does that have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor -- it does not? I'm asking the Prosecutors if that particular document has an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found Attachment 7 to your statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This attachment is a letter, is it not, that was sent to you by Rajko Kasagic on 4 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you received that letter, did you not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that letter talks about the reduction of staff at Atlas Prima Tours from 11 staff to 6, does it not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it informs you that the information that Mr. Kasagic has about that was based on complaints of employees dismissed from Atlas Prima Tours, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says that according to the information provided by these dismissed employees, that the remaining employees were two Muslims, two Croats, and two Yugoslavs. And you are accused in that letter of dismissing all of the Serbs and keeping two Muslims, two Croats, and two Yugoslavs; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin's name does not appear anywhere in this letter, does it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His signature doesn't appear on it anywhere, does it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to hand my copies of these to -- well, I better not do it that way. I want to make these documents exhibits, Your Honour. And the problem is that the copies I have I've made marks on, and I don't think I have a clean copy here with me today. If the registry could tell me an exhibit number, I could then put them in the record tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What marks have you made on them, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've got some underlining and then some yellow highlighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got clean copies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you prepared to make use of the clean copies that Ms. Sutherland can provide you with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course. That's no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And these will become --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: DB62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure Mr. Ackerman has a look at them and confirm for us that they are the same documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They're exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Better copies than I have, but otherwise the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So those will be DB62 and ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A and B. And Madam Registrar, please, if you could let us have copies of them at some point in time. In the meantime, while this is going on, Ms. Sutherland, we still don't have the list of the documents that you are going to make use of during the testimony of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It was that one bundle of documents provided by Ms. Gustin just before we started this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have distributed it to you. I left that on your bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the one with the discovery -- disclosure number 4.1255?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Thank you. Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us during your testimony that there were -- after 4 December 1991 and before 30 April 1992, that there were other articles, some newspaper articles, that appeared in the newspaper making -- written by journalists, making essentially the same allegation that you had dismissed the Serb staff and retained two Muslims, two Croats, and two Yugoslavs. That's a fair statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to now be provided with Prosecution's Exhibit 165. And this is the article that you were referring to where Mr. Brdjanin is speaking about the example of Atlas and how six employees were fired, all six of them Serbs. And what remained was two Muslims, two Croats, and two Yugoslavs, the same thing that all these other people had been saying. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he says. But what he's saying is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand it's your position that what all these people are saying is not correct. But I bet there is room in your mind for the possibility that what happened here was that incorrect information was given to Mr. Kasagic in December by one of your former employees, who said you had dismissed all Serbs, and the only people left were two Muslims, two Croats, and two Yugoslavs. That was then picked up by journalists and put in Glas that you had dismissed all the Serbs and that there were only two Muslims, two Croats, and two Yugoslavs left, and that Mr. Brdjanin heard about that from Glas, believed it to be true, and repeated it when he was interviewed. Now, that's a scenario that's probably true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. Everything started with Mr. Dragoljub Lukic's going to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And is it correct that the people remaining were two Muslims, two Croats, and two Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- when talking about ethnicity, the Yugoslav ethnicity was a product of which I too was a member, so that if we were to apply that principle, then there could be said to have been four Yugoslavs. However, as far as I know, both Mrs. Rada and Mrs. Tijana are of Serb ethnicity and not of Yugoslav ethnicity. Anyway, that nation no longer exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when this document from Mr. Kasagic refers to two Yugoslavs, it's actually referring to those two women who are of Serb ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Making it appear that you had fired all the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished with that document now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document, then, in this chain of documents was the decision of the Banja Luka War Staff of 8 May 1992, which you will recall said in paragraph 7: "In the future, tickets for flights to Belgrade may not be sold to persons without the approval of National Defence Councils. The work of the Atlas and Putnik travel agencies are to be placed under the control of the War Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Now, isn't it the case that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ackerman. Just for the record, that's Exhibit P179.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The decision of the 8th of May, 1992, 03-297/92 is that the one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 03-297/92. Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document which I'm informed is P179. Now, I want to ask you this question. You're familiar with what I'm talking about, are you not? Or do you need to see it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know, yes. I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that the only reason that the War Staff would become concerned about tickets being sold to persons without the approval of the National Defence Counsel, would be a concern whether it was correct or not that tickets were being sold to people for the purpose of assisting them in leaving the area and avoiding conscription?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. We sold tickets, but tickets were mostly not bought by those persons but by people representing them. Tickets are goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, surely the War Staff of ARK would not be placing your work under the control of the National Defence Council to prevent tickets being sold to non-Serb persons who wanted to leave the area, would they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any information about that, nor was there any kind of control. And I think there shouldn't have been any anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't make sense that there would have been a concern that persons were evading conscription at that time by buying tickets and going to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is sense, according to the decision and the opinion of the Crisis Staff, but the control as to whether someone can go or not is checked at the airport. Anyone can buy a ticket but at the check-in, that is where there were representatives of the army and the police who checked things, and they probably should have turned back people who did not have in their possession regular permission issued by the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it's conceivable that they could have been bribed by wealthy Serbs to allow their privileged sons to leave the area. Isn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the airport?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, at the airport.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look -- and again, I'm not certain about the exhibit number of this document. It's a document of -- well, War Staff/Crisis Staff conclusions of 9 May 1992, 03299/92.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P183.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask that you be shown this exhibit, because I think it's important you see this language. We haven't talked about it before. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in having you look at plaintiff's -- at Prosecutor's Exhibit 183, paragraph number 6. "Due to abuses in its work, the Atlas travel agency is prohibited from further work." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph: "The Putnik travel agency alone shall be allowed to sell tickets for flights to Belgrade." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next paragraph: "The above agency, referring obviously to Putnik, may not sell tickets to males aged between 18 and 60 unless they possess a certificate issued by the National Defence Council allowing them to leave the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." That's what it says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And doesn't that now make it clear that the concern of the Crisis Staff was that people were leaving who were subject to conscription and that they were trying to prevent that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to them, that was a reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this decision was issued on 9 May of 1992. And it said in paragraph 6 that "The Atlas travel agency is prohibited from further work." But Atlas travel agency continued to function after that, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the decision of the Crisis Staff had no effect or was ignored or something; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not ignored but in contact with certain persons in the municipality for a short while, they tacitly permitted it to go on working for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on now. And I'd ask you to be provided with Exhibit 532, Prosecution Exhibit 532. Do you have that? There are several things I want to ask you about it. This is a decision, is it not, of the Crisis Staff of 3 June 1992, making a second effort to terminate the operation of Atlas travel agency and ordering that it cease operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it is not a second decision. It's the first decision that we received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at the stamp at the bottom right-hand corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The stamp says that it is -- I think it says the Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it says the Autonomous Region of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it say anywhere on that stamp "the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina"?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does refer, does it not, to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the other thing I'd like you to notice is there is a signature on there. And in front of that signature, you should see the word "Za." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Za," means that it was signed by someone else for Mr. Brdjanin, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that now. I didn't pay any attention to that earlier on. But surely he wouldn't have signed it if it was not in agreement with Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that's something you don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it is the case that this decision was never published in the Official Gazette, might it not then be the case that it was never actually approved by Mr. Brdjanin and never became an official document of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is equally not in a position to answer that question on the same argument. You were perfectly right when you told him that's something you don't know. Do you? How can you expect him to be in a position to answer this question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Sir -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you proceed to your next question. Earlier on, sir, you said that you were asked whether this document says anywhere this Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And you said no. Unless you were referring to the stamp at the bottom of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We were referring to the stamp, Your Honour. That's what I was asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To the stamp, but not to the -- not to the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can he confirm to us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the heading itself, it does mention the Autonomous Region of Krajina and whether it also mentions Crisis Staff of -- situated in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is normal that the stamp need not go into detail. I know of a host of stamps. And every preamble, as in this case, refers to a part of the Autonomous Region, in this case the Crisis Staff, and that is what we find in the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, in the stamp itself, there are two sides to it. On one side, as I read it, it says "the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina"; is that correct? Or "Socialist Federation Republic of Yugoslavia"? Then -- can you look at that stamp again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On both sides -- on either side, there are three lines with words. Let's start with the one at the top. Can you translate -- can you read that out to us. It's "Socialist Federation of the Republics of Yugoslavia"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]"Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then the next line just below, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you read the next line, please, now. I can't read it myself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it repeated twice? The third line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Oh, I see. The third line. "Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's look. On the other side you have exactly a repetition of the same things, of the same names, or is it anything different, or is it just the same in Cyrillic script now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same thing. That was the regular practice in the case of all stamps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you do have a mention of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's back in your hands, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document we've been talking about is dated 3 June of 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document which terminates the operation of Atlas, ceases its operation, and places its premises at the disposal of the Municipal Assembly, and enters into force on the day of its adoption, 3 June 1992; yes?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, Atlas continued to function and ignored that decision.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't ignore it. But in a kind of agreement, if I can call it that, we continued working for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at this point, you weren't the director any more, were you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just advisor.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next thing that happened -- well, not the next thing, but a thing that happened after that was on 26 June of 1992, a letter was issued by Atlas Prima Tours travel agency, which had been ordered to cease operation on the 3rd of June. On the 26th of June, that travel agency issues a letter to you relieving you of your position with that agency, signed by Nada Crljenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if the decision of the Crisis Staff of 3 June and the one preceding that of 9 May had any force at all, there wasn't any Atlas Prima Tours for you to have been fired from. It shouldn't have been in operation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should -- that question should be asked of Mrs. Nada Crljenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the proposition that you were relieved based upon a decision of the Crisis Staff of 22 June makes absolutely no sense at all, because there wasn't any -- as far as a Crisis Staff was concerned, there wasn't any Atlas Prima Tours travel agency on 22 June 1992, was there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was fired, formally it did exist. And any consequences were borne by Mrs. Nada Crljenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. It's probably true that it did exist, because nobody was paying any attention to the decisions of this supposed ARK Crisis Staff or implementing them in any way. I want to show you -- I'm going to hand you -- the usher a document and have him give it to you. And what I'm giving you is simply a clean copy of what is Prosecution's Exhibit 535 but does not have any of the marks on it that you made Friday. Now, on there -- and I'd ask that you put it on the ELMO so we can follow the instructions that I'm going to give you. That's just magic. This works real good, Your Honour. With the Court's permission, I'm going to switch sides of the desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do whatever you like, Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I would like you to do is in the building -- the municipal building, skupstina opstina, I would like you to draw on there the location of the front doors of that building, the entry doors to that building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Let's do it this way. Let's do it in a different manner. Do you have an extra copy of P535?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Unmarked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I've given him, Your Honour, is an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you have given him an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is going to be a new exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's going to be a Defence exhibit when I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me give you a pen to draw it with. I don't like that pen. Give me that red pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has a marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That thing is like -- it's like killing a flea with a sledge hammer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The front doors of that building. That is the entry -- the entry doors to that building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Just for the record, what you've done is you first drew entry doors to the park and then realised you had the wrong building and then made the same kind of drawing down on the municipal building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you put your initials next to that mark over here -- over there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And can you cross out the other part which you marked in the park and put your initials there as well, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also what I would like you to do is put some kind of a designation next to where you've drawn the front door, your choice, that will show that what you have drawn there are the front doors. You can put "D" for door or whatever you want to put there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He knows English. He can write "doors."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, sir, did you write there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That works. All right. The second thing that I want you to -- this is kind of a redrawing. But I'd like you to again show us on the Atlas building where it was you could look out and see what was going on in the street outside. And you've initialed that, and it's the only mark on the atlas building; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to say yes so that --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All right. Now, that office that you had there was the director's office; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was located on what you call the first floor, which for those of us from the US, at least, understand is the second floor.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] First floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was actually one floor up from the ground, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] First floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But one floor up from the ground.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when Nada Crljenica replaced you as director of Atlas, then she took over that office and you didn't sit there anymore; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you continued to occupy the director's office?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You continued to occupy the director's office?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that in that municipal building, the Crisis Staff had offices in that building. Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the offices of the Crisis Staff in that building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But according to what people said, I know where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were on the second floor. I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you just told me you knew where they were. Now you're just guessing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say I knew but according to what people said when my employees went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many offices did the Crisis Staff have up there on the second floor?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I never went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were signs on the door saying "Crisis Staff Autonomous Region of Krajina" or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As I said, I never went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people worked for the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Chamber that you saw people going in and out of that building who were members of the Crisis Staff. You don't actually know, do you, sir, that they were going there or had been there to attend meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know that. But these were not employees of the Crisis Staff. I don't know how many were employees there. But these were members of that staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how could you tell they were actually going there to attend meetings of the staff? Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After any decision of the Crisis Staff, that was published the following morning. It was written in -- it was published in the Glas newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So because there was a decision published in Glas, you assume that people you saw going in and out of the building were going to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about a number of them being members of the Crisis Staff. But they also called to their meetings some other people as well, particularly some people who belonged to more famous Banja Luka firms. For instance, Mr. Kustrinovic and Mr. Lanovic [phoen], were not members of the Crisis Staff but they did go to meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to a Crisis Staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this being the municipal building for Banja Luka municipality, there were many, many people going out of that building on business of one form or another all day, every day; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- or did you know at that time the persons who were the presidents of the assembly or executive council of any of the other municipalities that were part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you didn't make these observations about who was coming and going from that building on a daily basis, did you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on Friday, I said it wasn't in a kind of inquisition that was constantly monitoring this. It just happened out of boredom because I had nothing to do. Occasionally I would through the window and I would see who was going in. And from the main members of the Crisis Staff, I saw people going in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us on Friday, sir, as a matter of fact, page 74 of the LiveNote: "I didn't observe this every morning. I had also other matters to attend to." And you were referring to Vojo Kupresanin. "I did see him at least a few times." That was your testimony, just to be fair to you, regarding my question. My next question is: To be able to see from your office people entering and leaving that building, you had to actually stand up and look out the window, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't something you could observe just while you were sitting at your desk, was it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's all the questions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Madam Fauveau, you're free to arrange -- I'm not quite sure whether you prefer to use the same place that Mr. Ackerman used for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I please give a number to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's the next DB -- DB number, 63, I think something like that. 63 or 64. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: DB63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 63. Mr. Ackerman, this diagram, sketch, is now DB63.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I offer that into evidence, then, Your Honour. And there was one other document, 62, that was identified today. I offer them both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, are you in a position to start?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps you can limit yourself to the preliminaries this next quarter of an hour, because that's all we have, less than that, and then you go to the substance tomorrow. Thank you. Madam Fauveau is the co-counsel for General Talic. And she will be cross-examining you now. Cross-examined by Ms. Fauveau-Ivanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Yesterday you spoke about a military lorry which was unloading weapons in front of your house. And you said that you were able to see even the number plates of that lorry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the numbers -- what were the letters that appeared on the number plates?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's hard to say now, but these were specific number plates of the former JNA. I know these number plates very well. And there's no doubt that this was a JNA lorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not recall the letters that appeared on the number plates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all the vehicles of the JNA have the same numbers on their number plates -- the letters?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The letters that appeared on the JNA vehicles were different, then. They were just denoting vehicles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The vehicle that belonged to the Territorial Defence, did they have a different number plate compared to the one that -- those that belonged to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no. I think they had the same registration plates. But I think it was -- there was an additional letter "T" or something like that. But that lorry was not Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of another occasion which happened in 1992 when a lorry was stopped in front of your house and that it was unloading boxes and crates in front of your house. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw this lorry unloading the crates in front of your house, and you were watching through the window; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. I remember as if it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you said that these weapons were distributed to uniquely Serbian apartments; is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to see to which apartments these weapons were distributed or delivered?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below my apartment I heard the door opening, and when the weapons were brought in and delivery of the weapons. And then I watched as they carried the crates into other entrances. It's a long building with several entrances. And I knew more or less who lived in the building, and I assumed -- or rather, I don't want to really say I was certain, but none of us received these weapons. We were never offered these weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. But you personally, you were not able to see to which apartments the weapons were delivered; is that correct? Physically you did not see it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw for the apartment that's below me, underneath mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see it or did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the opening of a door precisely at that very apartment -- of that very apartment. I saw somebody enter and somebody leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You heard them. But did you see them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them as they were entering into the building and when they left the entrance to the building. They were entering with and they were leaving without.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is very simple: Were you able to see the door of the apartment open and then close, the door of the apartment not of your building?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. But according to what I heard, I know that that was the apartment, because I didn't dare open the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yesterday you spoke of the SOS forces. And you said that you saw them beginning of April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Banja Luka during the referendum for Bosnia? Do you know when this referendum took place, first of all?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know precisely. Possibly in '90 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm speaking about the referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, about that referendum. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This referendum took place on the 29th of February, 1st of March, 1992, do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, were you in Banja Luka during those two days of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, did you see barricades anywhere in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in 1992, you did not know all the members of the Crisis Staff. Could you tell us the names of those that you are certain in 1992 that they were members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember some names. Puvacic, Kupresanin, Rosic, Erceg, and then the man from the police -- two of them, in fact, Zupljanin. I remember those names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about General Talic, and you said that you thought that his brother went to school with you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that. But I said I wasn't certain whether that was General Talic's brother's brother or his brother. I'm not sure about that. But that colleague of mine, who's a urologist, he's a medical specialist, he is in a hospital in Belgrade. He works in a hospital in Belgrade. And the last time I saw him was at the celebration of the finals, school finals in Banja Luka, sometime in the 1980s, at the -- in late 1980s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that this person has absolutely no connection to General Talic, would you still be certain that the person that you saw twice enter the municipality building was General Talic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw General Talic enter the municipality building twice. Could you give us more specific detail on the period.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of very intense sessions of the Crisis Staff, and Mr. Talic was himself a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But here two minutes ago, you did not mention him.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you will allow me that I cannot immediately remember all the names. I would have remembered perhaps more names in the meantime. I can't say that I'm a computer who can just type it in and then produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I think we can stop here for today, if that's convenient with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just -- I have two more questions, so that I can finish with this topic, if Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992, did you know that General Talic was a member of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Crisis Staff? In 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still have before you your written statement that you gave to the Prosecutor's office in May 2001?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look on page 7. It's on the third paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the third paragraph at the end in B/C/S. You spoke about the members of the Crisis Staff. And you said: [In English] "I saw other Serbs enter the building, such as Rajko Kasagic, Momir Talic, and Predrag Radic, but I'm not sure they were Crisis Staff members."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when you gave this statement, you were not certain that General Talic was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not certain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And today? Why are you certain today?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the meantime, I had the opportunity to look at class newspaper issues, which I -- while I was in Banja Luka was not able to have before me. And that's how I acquired this knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to return to my first question. In 1992, when you were in Banja Luka, did you know that General Talic was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I continue tomorrow? Mr. President, I think I only have 20 minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So prepare yourselves for the next witness. I suppose he should be here from the beginning of the session. Keep him separate from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So once more, I thank the interpreters, the technicians and everyone. We'll meet tomorrow afternoon at 2.15, like today, in this courtroom, Courtroom I. Good evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please escort the witness out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
